title: "C Conditional Statements"
---

## Description

This is the second notebook. It covers decision-making in C, starting with comparison and logical results, then moving through `if`, `else`, and `else if`, nested decisions, small menu and game projects, and finally the `switch` statement.

## How to use the pack

Work through the exercises in order, since later ones build on earlier ones. Attempt the Questions before revealing the answer. If a solution is unclear, ask LLMs for a step-by-step explanation.

## Part 1 — Comparison and Logical Results

In C, a true comparison or logical expression has the value `1`, and a false one has the value `0`.

### 1. Comparison Results
**Question:** Predict the output.

**The Code:**
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a = 5, b = 8;
    printf("%d\n", a < b);
    printf("%d\n", a == b);
    printf("%d\n", a + b > 10);
    return 0;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
**Output:**
```text
1
0
1
```
`5 < 8` is true, `5 == 8` is false, and `a + b` is `13`, which is greater than `10`.
:::

### 2. AND, OR, and NOT
**Question:** Predict the output.

**The Code:**
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int x = 6;
    printf("%d\n", (x > 3) && (x < 10));
    printf("%d\n", (x < 3) || (x == 6));
    printf("%d\n", !(x == 6));
    printf("%d\n", (x >= 6) && (x != 7));
    return 0;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
**Output:**
```text
1
1
0
1
```
`&&` needs both sides true, `||` needs at least one side true, and `!` reverses a truth value.
:::

### 3. Mixing `&&` and `||` (Optional)
**Question:** Predict the output. `&&` is evaluated before `||` unless parentheses change the order.

**The Code:**
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a = 2, b = 7;

    printf("%d\n", a > 5 || b > 5 && a > 5);
    printf("%d\n", (a > 5 || b > 5) && a > 1);
    printf("%d\n", a < b && b < 10 || a == 0);
    return 0;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
**Output:**
```text
0
1
1
```
Line 1: `b > 5 && a > 5` is `1 && 0`, which is `0`, and `a > 5` is also `0`, so the result is `0 || 0`. Line 2: the parentheses make `(0 || 1)` happen first, giving `1 && 1`. Line 3: `a < b && b < 10` is true, so the whole expression is `1`.
:::

## Part 2 — `if` and `else`

### 4. Positive, Negative, or Zero
**Question:** Read an integer. Print `Positive`, `Negative`, or `Zero`.

**Example Input:**
```text
-4
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter an integer: Negative
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int number;
    printf("Enter an integer: ");
    scanf("%d", &number);

    if (number > 0) {
        printf("Positive\n");
    } else if (number < 0) {
        printf("Negative\n");
    } else {
        printf("Zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
With input `7` the program prints `Positive`, and with `0` it prints `Zero`.
:::

### 5. Even or Odd
**Question:** Read an integer and print whether it is `Even` or `Odd`. Use the remainder operator `%`.

**Example Input:**
```text
7
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter an integer: Odd
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int number;
    printf("Enter an integer: ");
    scanf("%d", &number);

    if (number % 2 == 0) {
        printf("Even\n");
    } else {
        printf("Odd\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
Test for even with `== 0`. For negative numbers, `-3 % 2` is `-1` in C, so a test like `number % 2 == 1` would wrongly call `-3` even.
:::

### 6. Compare Two Numbers
**Question:** Read two integers. Print which one is larger, using the format shown, or print `Equal` if they have the same value.

**Example Input:**
```text
12 9
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter two integers: 12 is larger
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a, b;
    printf("Enter two integers: ");
    scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);

    if (a > b) {
        printf("%d is larger\n", a);
    } else if (b > a) {
        printf("%d is larger\n", b);
    } else {
        printf("Equal\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
With input `5 5` the program prints `Equal`.
:::

### 7. Inside a Range
**Question:** Read an integer. Print `Inside` if it is between **10 and 20 inclusive**, otherwise print `Outside`.

**Example Input:**
```text
15
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter an integer: Inside
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int number;
    printf("Enter an integer: ");
    scanf("%d", &number);

    if (number >= 10 && number <= 20) {
        printf("Inside\n");
    } else {
        printf("Outside\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
Both conditions must be true, so they are joined with `&&`. Writing `10 <= number <= 20` does not work in C.
:::

### 8. Admission Rule (Optional)
**Question:** Read an age and an entrance-test score. Print `Eligible` only if the age is at least `18` **and** the score is at least `60`. Otherwise print `Not eligible`.

**Example Input:**
```text
19 72
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter age and test score: Eligible
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int age, score;
    printf("Enter age and test score: ");
    scanf("%d %d", &age, &score);

    if (age >= 18 && score >= 60) {
        printf("Eligible\n");
```

:::

### 9. Score to Grade
**Question:** Read a score from `0` to `100` and print the grade: `A` for 90–100, `B` for 80–89, `C` for 70–79, `D` for 60–69, and `F` for 0–59. For a score below `0` or above `100`, print `Invalid score`. Use an `if` / `else if` ladder.

**Example Input:**
```text
85
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter a score (0-100): B
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int score;
    printf("Enter a score (0-100): ");
    scanf("%d", &score);

    if (score < 0 || score > 100) {
        printf("Invalid score\n");
    } else if (score >= 90) {
        printf("A\n");
    } else if (score >= 80) {
        printf("B\n");
    } else if (score >= 70) {
        printf("C\n");
    } else if (score >= 60) {
        printf("D\n");
    } else {
        printf("F\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
The ladder is checked from top to bottom and stops at the first true condition. That is why `score >= 80` does not also need `score < 90`.
:::

## Part 3 — Reading `if` / `else` Code

### 10. Two `if` Statements in a Row
**Question:** Predict the output. Pay attention to which `if` the `else` belongs to.

**The Code:**
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n = 4;
    if (n > 0)
        printf("A");
    if (n % 2 == 0)
        printf("B");
    else
        printf("C");
    printf("D\n");
    return 0;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
**Output:**
```text
ABD
```
The first `if` is separate and prints `A`. The `else` belongs to the second `if`; since `4` is even, `B` prints and `C` is skipped. `D` always prints.
:::

### 11. Which Branch Runs?
**Question:** Predict the output.

**The Code:**
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int score = 76;
    if (score >= 90)
        printf("Excellent\n");
    else if (score >= 70)
        printf("Good\n");
    else
        printf("Keep practising\n");
    return 0;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
**Output:**
```text
Good
```
`76` is not at least `90`, but it is at least `70`, so the second branch runs and the rest are skipped.
:::

### 12. Missing Braces (Optional)
**Question:** Predict the output. Ignore the indentation and read the code the way the compiler does.

**The Code:**
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int x = 3;
    if (x > 5)
        printf("A\n");
        printf("B\n");
    printf("C\n");
    return 0;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
**Output:**
```text
B
C
```
Without braces, an `if` controls only the next statement. `printf("B\n");` is not part of the `if`, so it always runs. Using braces `{ }` on every `if` avoids this trap.
:::

## Part 4 — Combined and Nested Decisions

### 13. Sign First, Then Parity
**Question:** Read an integer. First print whether it is `Positive`, `Negative`, or `Zero`. If it is positive, also print on a second line whether it is `Even` or `Odd`. Use a nested `if` inside the positive branch.

**Example Input:**
```text
8
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter an integer: Positive
Even
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int number;
    printf("Enter an integer: ");
    scanf("%d", &number);

    if (number > 0) {
        printf("Positive\n");
        if (number % 2 == 0) {
            printf("Even\n");
        } else {
            printf("Odd\n");
        }
    } else if (number < 0) {
        printf("Negative\n");
    } else {
        printf("Zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
:::

### 14. Largest of Three Numbers
**Question:** Read three integers and print the largest. Use nested `if` / `else` statements. Do not use arrays or loops.

**Example Input:**
```text
4 17 9
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter three integers: Largest: 17
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a, b, c, largest;
    printf("Enter three integers: ");
    scanf("%d %d %d", &a, &b, &c);

    if (a >= b) {
        if (a >= c) {
            largest = a;
        } else {
            largest = c;
        }
    } else {
        if (b >= c) {
            largest = b;
        } else {
            largest = c;
        }
    }

    printf("Largest: %d\n", largest);
    return 0;
}
```
The first comparison removes one candidate, and the nested `if` compares the winner with the third number. Using `>=` makes ties print the tied value.
:::

### 15. Leap Year
**Question:** Read a year. Print `Leap year` if it is divisible by `400`, or if it is divisible by `4` but not by `100`. Otherwise print `Not a leap year`.

**Example Input:**
```text
2024
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter a year: Leap year
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int year;
    printf("Enter a year: ");
    scanf("%d", &year);

    if (year % 400 == 0 || (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0)) {
        printf("Leap year\n");
    } else {
        printf("Not a leap year\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
`2000` is a leap year (divisible by `400`), but `1900` is not (divisible by `100` and not by `400`).
:::

### 16. Triangle Check (Optional)
**Question:** Read three positive integers as side lengths. A triangle is possible only if the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side. Print `Valid triangle` or `Not a triangle`.

**Example Input:**
```text
3 4 8
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter three side lengths: Not a triangle
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a, b, c;
    printf("Enter three side lengths: ");
    scanf("%d %d %d", &a, &b, &c);

    if (a + b > c && a + c > b && b + c > a) {
        printf("Valid triangle\n");
    } else {
        printf("Not a triangle\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
`3 + 4` is `7`, which is not greater than `8`, so the first condition fails. With input `3 4 5` the program prints `Valid triangle`.
:::

### 17. Ticket Price (Optional)
**Question:** Read an age and print the ticket price: under `6` is `Free`, `6` to `17` costs `5 EUR`, `18` to `64` costs `10 EUR`, and `65` or older costs `6 EUR`. A negative age prints `Invalid age`. Use the output format shown.

**Example Input:**
```text
12
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter age: Price: 5 EUR
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int age;
    printf("Enter age: ");
    scanf("%d", &age);

    if (age < 0) {
        printf("Invalid age\n");
    } else if (age < 6) {
        printf("Price: Free\n");
    } else if (age < 18) {
        printf("Price: 5 EUR\n");
    } else if (age < 65) {
        printf("Price: 10 EUR\n");
    } else {
        printf("Price: 6 EUR\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
Because the ladder stops at the first true condition, each branch only needs the upper limit of its age group.
:::

## Part 5 — Small Decision-Making Projects

### 18. Basic Calculator
**Question:** Read two numbers and an operator character (`+`, `-`, `*`, or `/`) in the form `number operator number`. Print the result with two decimal places. If the operator is `/` and the second number is zero, print `Cannot divide by zero`. For any other operator, print `Unknown operator`.

**Example Input:**
```text
9 * 2.5
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter: number operator number: Result: 22.50
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    double a, b;
    char op;
    printf("Enter: number operator number: ");
    scanf("%lf %c %lf", &a, &op, &b);

    if (op == '+') {
        printf("Result: %.2f\n", a + b);
    } else if (op == '-') {
        printf("Result: %.2f\n", a - b);
    } else if (op == '*') {
        printf("Result: %.2f\n", a * b);
    } else if (op == '/') {
        if (b == 0.0) {
            printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
        } else {
            printf("Result: %.2f\n", a / b);
        }
    } else {
        printf("Unknown operator\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
Check for division by zero before dividing. With input `7 / 0` the program prints `Cannot divide by zero`.
:::

### 19. Length Converter Menu
**Question:** Show the menu below, then read the choice and a value, and print the converted value with two decimal places. For any other choice, print `Invalid choice` and stop.

- `1` converts centimetres to metres
- `2` converts metres to centimetres
- `3` converts kilometres to metres

**Example Input:**
```text
1
250
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
1: cm to m
2: m to cm
3: km to m
Choice: Enter value: Result: 2.50 m
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int choice;
    double value;

    printf("1: cm to m\n2: m to cm\n3: km to m\nChoice: ");
    scanf("%d", &choice);

    if (choice < 1 || choice > 3) {
        printf("Invalid choice\n");
        return 0;
    }

    printf("Enter value: ");
    scanf("%lf", &value);

    if (choice == 1) {
        printf("Result: %.2f m\n", value / 100.0);
    } else if (choice == 2) {
        printf("Result: %.2f cm\n", value * 100.0);
    } else {
        printf("Result: %.2f m\n", value * 1000.0);
    }
    return 0;
}
```
Rejecting an invalid choice first with `return 0;` means the rest of the program only handles valid choices.
:::

### 20. Temperature Converter Menu (Optional)
**Question:** Show the menu below, then read the choice and a temperature and print the result with two decimal places. Use `F = C * 9 / 5 + 32` and `C = (F - 32) * 5 / 9`. For any other choice, print `Invalid choice`.

- `1` converts Celsius to Fahrenheit
- `2` converts Fahrenheit to Celsius

**Example Input:**
```text
1
100
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
1: Celsius to Fahrenheit
2: Fahrenheit to Celsius
Choice: Enter temperature: Result: 212.00 F
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int choice;
    double temperature;

    printf("1: Celsius to Fahrenheit\n2: Fahrenheit to Celsius\nChoice: ");
    scanf("%d", &choice);

    if (choice != 1 && choice != 2) {
        printf("Invalid choice\n");
        return 0;
    }

    printf("Enter temperature: ");
    scanf("%lf", &temperature);

    if (choice == 1) {
        printf("Result: %.2f F\n", temperature * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0);
    } else {
        printf("Result: %.2f C\n", (temperature - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0);
    }
    return 0;
}
```
Use `9.0 / 5.0` and not `9 / 5`: integer division would turn `9 / 5` into `1`.
:::

### 21. Two-Player Rock, Paper, Scissors
**Question:** Read one lowercase character per player: `r` for rock, `p` for paper, `s` for scissors. Print `Player 1 wins`, `Player 2 wins`, or `Draw`. If either character is invalid, print `Invalid choice`. Use conditions and logical operators.

**Example Input:**
```text
r
s
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Player 1 (r/p/s): Player 2 (r/p/s): Player 1 wins
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    char p1, p2;
    printf("Player 1 (r/p/s): ");
    scanf(" %c", &p1);
    printf("Player 2 (r/p/s): ");
    scanf(" %c", &p2);

    if ((p1 != 'r' && p1 != 'p' && p1 != 's') ||
        (p2 != 'r' && p2 != 'p' && p2 != 's')) {
        printf("Invalid choice\n");
    } else if (p1 == p2) {
        printf("Draw\n");
    } else if ((p1 == 'r' && p2 == 's') ||
               (p1 == 'p' && p2 == 'r') ||
               (p1 == 's' && p2 == 'p')) {
        printf("Player 1 wins\n");
    } else {
        printf("Player 2 wins\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
Handle invalid input first, then draws, then list the three ways Player 1 can win. Everything else must be a Player 2 win.
:::

## Part 6 — The `switch` Statement

A `switch` compares one value against several `case` labels. Each case normally ends with `break`, and `default` handles every other value.

### 22. Day of the Week
**Question:** Read a number from `1` to `7` and print the day name, with `1` as `Monday`. For any other number, print `Invalid day`. Use `switch`.

**Example Input:**
```text
3
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter a day number (1-7): Wednesday
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int day;
    printf("Enter a day number (1-7): ");
    scanf("%d", &day);

    switch (day) {
        case 1: printf("Monday\n"); break;
        case 2: printf("Tuesday\n"); break;
        case 3: printf("Wednesday\n"); break;
        case 4: printf("Thursday\n"); break;
        case 5: printf("Friday\n"); break;
        case 6: printf("Saturday\n"); break;
        case 7: printf("Sunday\n"); break;
        default: printf("Invalid day\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
:::

### 23. Missing `break`
**Question:** Predict the output. What happens when a `case` has no `break`?

**The Code:**
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n = 2;
    switch (n) {
        case 1:
            printf("one\n");
        case 2:
            printf("two\n");
        case 3:
            printf("three\n");
            break;
        case 4:
            printf("four\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
**Output:**
```text
two
three
```
The program jumps to `case 2` and keeps running every following statement until it reaches a `break`. This is called fall-through. It stops after `three` because of the `break` there.
:::

### 24. Vowel or Consonant
**Question:** Read a lowercase letter and print `Vowel` for `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u`, otherwise `Consonant`. Use `switch` with several `case` labels sharing one block of code.

**Example Input:**
```text
e
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter a lowercase letter: Vowel
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    char letter;
    printf("Enter a lowercase letter: ");
    scanf(" %c", &letter);

    switch (letter) {
        case 'a':
        case 'e':
        case 'i':
        case 'o':
        case 'u':
            printf("Vowel\n");
            break;
        default:
            printf("Consonant\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
Fall-through is useful here: the empty cases `a`, `e`, `i`, and `o` fall through to the shared `printf`.
:::

### 25. Calculator with `switch` (Optional)
**Question:** Rewrite the calculator from Question 18 using `switch` on the operator character.

**Example Input:**
```text
8 / 2
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter: number operator number: Result: 4.00
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    double a, b;
    char op;
    printf("Enter: number operator number: ");
    scanf("%lf %c %lf", &a, &op, &b);

    switch (op) {
        case '+':
            printf("Result: %.2f\n", a + b);
            break;
        case '-':
            printf("Result: %.2f\n", a - b);
            break;
        case '*':
            printf("Result: %.2f\n", a * b);
            break;
        case '/':
            if (b == 0.0) {
                printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
            } else {
                printf("Result: %.2f\n", a / b);
            }
            break;
        default:
            printf("Unknown operator\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
`switch` works with integers and characters, not with ranges such as `score >= 90`. Ranges still need `if` / `else if`.
:::

## Part 7 — Mixed Practice

### 26. Final Challenge — Fizz Buzz Check
**Question:** Read an integer. If it is divisible by both `3` and `5`, print `FizzBuzz`. If it is divisible only by `3`, print `Fizz`. If it is divisible only by `5`, print `Buzz`. Otherwise, print the number itself.

**Example Input:**
```text
15
```

**Expected Program Output** (not counting the characters typed by the user):
```text
Enter an integer: FizzBuzz
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n;
    printf("Enter an integer: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    if (n % 3 == 0 && n % 5 == 0) {
        printf("FizzBuzz\n");
    } else if (n % 3 == 0) {
        printf("Fizz\n");
    } else if (n % 5 == 0) {
        printf("Buzz\n");
    } else {
        printf("%d\n", n);
    }
    return 0;
}
```
The combined test must come first. Otherwise `15` would match `n % 3 == 0` and print only `Fizz`. With input `9` the program prints `Fizz`, with `10` it prints `Buzz`, and with `7` it prints `7`.
:::
